about: Cycling history places a rider can pass on a ride, world wide. Hand-written; tools/wikimedia/cycling_history.py locates each one and writes out/cycling-history.json for app:catalog:seed-cycling-history. `osm` is the exact OSM object (its point wins), `qid` the Wikidata item, `wiki` an English Wikipedia title when neither is known yet. `about` names the English Wikipedia articles of the people or events the story is about; `kind` is a PlaceKind of letter Q; `year` is when the story happened (it puts the place on the timeline); `photo` is a Commons file a person looked at (it shows the place, no person close up); `story` is what the rider reads.

places.name: Technoseum
places.story: Mannheim's state museum of technology and work. Mannheim is the city of the first ride on a two-wheeler: Karl Drais set off from here on his running machine on 12 June 1817.

places.name: Karl Drais monument, Karlsruhe
places.story: Karl Drais, inventor of the running machine of 1817 that became the bicycle, was born in Karlsruhe in 1785. His home town raised this monument to him.

places.name: Karl Drais monument, Rheinau
places.story: On 12 June 1817 Karl Drais rode his running machine from Mannheim to the Schwetzingen relay house, in today's Rheinau, and back: the first recorded ride on a two-wheeler. This monument in Rheinau remembers it.

places.name: Coventry Transport Museum
places.story: Coventry was the cradle of the British cycle industry. James Starley built wheels and tricycles here, and his nephew John Kemp Starley made the Rover safety bicycle in 1885, the shape every bicycle still has.

places.name: Raleigh Street
places.story: The Raleigh Bicycle Company takes its name from this street, where its first small workshop made bicycles in the 1880s.

places.name: Monument to the Michaux
places.story: Pierre Michaux was born in Bar-le-Duc. In Paris in the 1860s he and his son Ernest put pedals on the front wheel and built the velocipede in series. The town raised this monument to them in 1894.

places.name: Courthill Smithy
places.story: The blacksmith Kirkpatrick Macmillan worked at this smithy. Local history credits him with a rear-wheel bicycle driven by treadles and rods around 1839, years before pedals came.

places.name: Parc de Saint-Cloud
places.story: On 31 May 1868 a bicycle race over 1,200 metres was held in this park. The Englishman James Moore won it, in one of the first bicycle races on record.

places.name: Le Réveil Matin
places.story: The first Tour de France started here, in front of the Réveil Matin inn, on 1 July 1903. Sixty riders set off towards Lyon; Maurice Garin won the race.

places.name: Piazzale Loreto
places.story: The first Giro d'Italia started from this square in the early morning of 13 May 1909. Luigi Ganna won it.

places.name: Parc des Princes
places.story: This ground opened in 1897 as a velodrome. The Tour de France finished on its track every year from 1903 to 1967.

places.name: Vélodrome Jacques-Anquetil
places.story: La Cipale velodrome in the Bois de Vincennes was the finish of the Tour de France from 1968 to 1974, before the race moved to the Champs-Elysees in 1975.

places.name: Champs-Élysées
places.story: The Tour de France has finished on this avenue since 1975. In 2022 the first stage of the new Tour de France Femmes finished here too.

places.name: Memorial of the Vel' d'Hiv Roundup
places.story: The Vélodrome d'Hiver, Paris's indoor cycling track, stood near here. In July 1942 the police held more than 8,000 Jews in it, many of them children, before their deportation. This memorial remembers them.

places.name: Vélodrome André-Pétrieux
places.story: Paris-Roubaix has finished on this open-air track in most years since 1943. In the old shower block each cubicle carries a plaque with the name of a winner.

places.name: Trouée d'Arenberg
places.story: This cobbled road through the Arenberg forest entered Paris-Roubaix in 1968. Jean Stablinski, who had worked in the coal mine under it, proposed it to the organisers.

places.name: Musée de l'Aventure Peugeot
places.story: Peugeot made bicycles from 1882, long before its first car. The family firm's museum in Sochaux shows its bicycles as well as its cars.

places.name: Eugène Christophe memorial
places.story: In the 1913 Tour de France Eugène Christophe broke his fork on the Tourmalet. Rules said he had to repair it himself, so he walked down to the forge in this village and welded it. This memorial marks the place.

places.name: Le Géant du Tourmalet
places.story: The Tour de France first crossed the Tourmalet in 1910, and Octave Lapize was first over the top. The statue of a rider at the summit, the Géant du Tourmalet, remembers that day.

places.name: Monument to Henri Desgrange
places.story: Henri Desgrange founded the Tour de France in 1903. He wrote that next to the Galibier the other big climbs were 'pale and vulgar beer'. His monument stands near the tunnel on the south side.

places.name: Tom Simpson memorial
places.story: On 13 July 1967 the British rider Tom Simpson collapsed and died here, about a kilometre below the top of Mont Ventoux, during the Tour de France. Riders often leave a bidon or a cap at his memorial.

places.name: Fabio Casartelli memorial
places.story: The Italian Olympic champion Fabio Casartelli died after a crash on this descent of the Col de Portet d'Aspet on 18 July 1995, during the Tour de France.

places.name: Coppi and Bobet memorial
places.story: In the rocks of the Casse Déserte a plaque remembers Fausto Coppi and Louison Bobet, who both won the Tour de France with attacks on the Izoard. Bobet rode away here in 1953 on his way to his first win.

places.name: Wim van Est memorial
places.story: In 1951 Wim van Est became the first Dutchman to wear the yellow jersey. The next day he fell about 70 metres into the ravine here on the Aubisque descent and survived. A plaque marks the bend.

places.name: Notre-Dame des Cyclistes
places.story: A chapel for cyclists, opened in 1959. Riders and teams give it their jerseys, and it keeps them with the bicycles of famous riders.

places.name: Madonna del Ghisallo
places.photo: Magreglio Santuario di Madonna di Ghisallo Esterno Facciata 3.jpg
places.story: In 1949 Pope Pius XII named the Madonna del Ghisallo patroness of cyclists. The chapel at the top of the climb keeps bicycles and jerseys of champions.

places.name: Casa Coppi
places.story: Fausto Coppi was born in this house in 1919. He won the Giro d'Italia five times and the Tour de France twice. He and his brother Serse are buried in the village.

places.name: Museo dei Campionissimi
places.story: Costante Girardengo, the first rider called campionissimo, was born in Novi Ligure in 1893, and Fausto Coppi lived here. The museum of the champions tells their story.

places.name: Gino Bartali cycling museum
places.story: Gino Bartali was born in Ponte a Ema in 1914 and won the Tour de France in 1938 and 1948. During the war he carried false papers for Jews in the frame of his bicycle. Yad Vashem named him Righteous Among the Nations in 2013.

places.name: Spazio Pantani
places.story: Marco Pantani grew up in Cesenatico and trained in the hills behind it. In 1998 he won the Giro d'Italia and the Tour de France. This museum keeps his bicycles and jerseys.

places.name: Marco Pantani monument
places.story: Marco Pantani made his name on the Mortirolo in the 1994 Giro d'Italia, when he rode away from the best riders in the world. This monument remembers him.

places.name: Velodromo Vigorelli
places.story: On this wooden track Fausto Coppi set the hour record in 1942 and Jacques Anquetil in 1956. In 1958 Elsy Jacobs of Luxembourg set the first women's hour record here.

places.name: Velodrome Suisse
places.story: Filippo Ganna set the hour record here on 8 October 2022 with 56.792 km. Earlier the same year, on 23 May, Ellen van Dijk set the women's record on the same track with 49.254 km.

places.name: UCI World Cycling Centre
places.story: The Union Cycliste Internationale, founded in Paris in 1900, has had its seat and its training centre with a velodrome here in Aigle since 2002.

places.name: Eddy Merckx metro station
places.story: This metro station carries the name of Eddy Merckx, five times winner of the Tour de France. Under glass in the station stands the bicycle on which he set the hour record in Mexico City in 1972.

places.name: Velódromo Olímpico Agustín Melgar
places.photo: Vista aérea del Velódromo Olímpico Agustín Melgar y sus alrededores 01.jpg
places.story: Built for the 1968 Olympics, at 2,240 metres altitude. Eddy Merckx set the hour record here on 25 October 1972, Francesco Moser beat it in 1984, and Leontien van Moorsel set the women's record here in 2003.

places.name: Centrum Ronde van Vlaanderen
places.story: The museum of the Tour of Flanders, in the town where the race now finishes. It tells the story of the race since 1913 and of the cobbled climbs around it.

places.name: KOERS. Museum of Cycle Racing
places.story: The Belgian museum of road cycling, in the town where many Flemish riders grew up. It shows bicycles, jerseys and the history of the sport.

places.name: Kuipke
places.story: The tight indoor track of Ghent. The Six Days of Ghent are raced here every November.

places.name: Velorama
places.story: The Dutch national bicycle museum, on the Waal quay in Nijmegen. It shows the bicycle from the draisine of 1817 to today.

places.name: Hovenring
places.story: A ring for cyclists that hangs from a 70 metre pylon above a busy road junction. It opened in 2012 and lets riders cross without meeting cars.

places.name: Hoge Veluwe National Park
places.story: Since 1974 the park lends its free white bicycles to every visitor. Today about 1,800 of them stand ready at the entrances.

places.name: Cykelslangen
places.story: The Bicycle Snake, a winding orange bridge only for cyclists, opened in 2014 above the harbour quay. It became a picture of Copenhagen as a cycling city.

places.name: Herne Hill Velodrome
places.story: Opened in 1891, one of the oldest cycle tracks in the world still in use. It held the track events of the 1948 Olympic Games.

places.name: Lee Valley VeloPark
places.story: Built for the 2012 Olympic Games. Bradley Wiggins set the hour record on this track on 7 June 2015 with 54.526 km.

places.name: National Cycling Centre
places.story: Opened in 1994 as the first indoor Olympic velodrome in Britain. The British track team that won so many medals from 2008 trained here.

places.name: Beryl Burton Gardens
places.story: Beryl Burton of Morley won seven world titles and was British best all-rounder 25 years in a row. In 1967 her 12-hour ride was longer than the men's record. This street in her home town carries her name.

places.name: Senate House, Cambridge
places.story: On 21 May 1897, while the university voted on degrees for women, students hung a figure of a woman on a bicycle from a window opposite. The bicycle had become a sign of women's freedom.

places.name: Vikingskipet
places.story: For the 1993 world championships this skating hall got a cycle track. On it the Scot Graeme Obree set the hour record on 17 July 1993, on a bicycle he built himself.

places.name: Vélodrome de Bordeaux
places.story: Chris Boardman set the hour record on this track in July 1993, a week after Graeme Obree. Miguel Induráin set it here in September 1994.

places.name: Wright Cycle Company
places.story: Wilbur and Orville Wright repaired, built and sold bicycles in this shop from 1895. The bicycle trade paid for their flying experiments.

places.name: Major Taylor statue
places.story: Marshall 'Major' Taylor of Worcester won the world sprint title in 1899, the first African-American cycling world champion, while he met racism on and off the track. The city raised this statue in 2008.

places.name: Major Taylor Velodrome
places.story: Major Taylor was born in Indianapolis in 1878 and became the world sprint champion in 1899. This track in his city carries his name.

places.name: Fort Missoula
places.story: In 1897 the 25th Infantry Bicycle Corps, Black soldiers of the US Army, rode from this fort to St. Louis, about 1,900 miles, to test the bicycle for the army.

places.name: Madison Square
places.photo: Madison Square Park from Above at Night New York City.jpg
places.story: The first Madison Square Garden stood on the northeast corner of this square. Its six-day races of the 1890s gave the track race for teams of two its name: the madison.

places.name: Ocean Parkway
places.story: In 1894 a path along this parkway opened for cyclists only. It is called the first designated bicycle path in the United States.

places.name: Bicycle Museum of America
places.story: A museum in New Bremen, Ohio, with American bicycles from the boneshaker and the high-wheeler to the bikes of today.

places.name: Dunc Gray Velodrome
places.story: The track of the 2000 Sydney Olympics. It carries the name of Dunc Gray, who won Australia's first Olympic cycling gold in 1932.

places.name: Kitakyushu Media Dome
places.story: Keirin racing began in Kokura in November 1948. This dome is Kokura's keirin track today. Keirin became an Olympic event in 2000.

places.name: Shimano Bicycle Museum
places.story: Sakai, a town of knife and gun makers, became the centre of the Japanese bicycle trade, and Shimano was founded here in 1921. Its museum shows the bicycle from the draisine to today.

places.name: Africa Rising Cycling Center
places.story: The base of Team Rwanda, set up with the American rider Jock Boyer, first American in the Tour de France. Riders from here raced the Tour du Rwanda and the world championships.

places.name: Mount Royal
places.story: The 1974 road world championships were raced over this mountain. Eddy Merckx won his third world title here.

places.name: Shay Elliott memorial
places.story: Shay Elliott of Dublin won stages in the Giro d'Italia, the Tour de France and the Vuelta, and in 1963 he became the first Irish rider to wear the yellow jersey. This memorial remembers him.

places.name: Eddy Merckx sculpture, Kiezegem
places.story: Eddy Merckx was born in Meensel-Kiezegem on 17 June 1945. He won the Tour de France and the Giro d'Italia five times each, and more races than any other professional rider.

places.name: Briek Schotte memorial
places.story: Briek Schotte was born in Kanegem in 1919. He won the Tour of Flanders in 1942 and 1948 and the world title in 1948 and 1950. Flemish cycling calls him the last of the Flandriens.

places.name: Stan Ockers monument
places.story: Stan Ockers won Liège-Bastogne-Liège and the world title in 1955. He died after a crash on the Antwerp track in 1956. His monument stands on the Côte des Forges, a climb of Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

places.name: Louison Bobet museum
places.story: Louison Bobet was born in Saint-Méen-le-Grand in 1925. In 1955 he became the first rider to win the Tour de France three years in a row. His home town keeps a museum about him.

places.name: Ottavio Bottecchia monument
places.story: Ottavio Bottecchia was the first Italian to win the Tour de France, in 1924, and he won it again in 1925. In June 1927 he was found badly hurt by this road at Peonis and died days later. How it happened was never cleared up.

places.name: Plaza Miguel Induráin
places.story: Miguel Induráin was born in Villava in 1964. He won the Tour de France five years in a row, from 1991 to 1995, and the Giro d'Italia in 1992 and 1993. His town named this square after him.

places.name: Sean Kelly Square
places.story: Sean Kelly of Carrick-on-Suir won Paris-Nice seven years in a row, from 1982 to 1988, and the Vuelta a España in 1988. His town named this square after him.

places.name: Lucho Herrera monument
places.story: Luis 'Lucho' Herrera of Fusagasugá won the Vuelta a España in 1987, the first Grand Tour won by a Colombian. He was best climber in the Tour de France, the Giro d'Italia and the Vuelta.

places.name: Massachusetts State House
places.story: On 25 June 1894 Annie Londonderry, a young mother from Boston, set off from here to ride around the world on a bicycle. She was back in the United States about 15 months later.

places.name: Kittie Knox Bike Path
places.story: Kittie Knox was a Black racing cyclist from Boston in the 1890s. When the League of American Wheelmen barred Black members in 1894, she rode to its 1895 meet with her membership card anyway. This path carries her name.

places.name: Frances Willard House
places.story: Frances Willard, who fought for women's votes, learned to ride a bicycle at 53. In 1895 she wrote a book about it, A Wheel Within a Wheel. This was her home.

places.name: Susan B. Anthony House
places.story: Susan B. Anthony, who fought for women's votes, lived in this house. In 1896 she said that the bicycle had done more to free women than anything else in the world.

places.name: Via Alfonsina Strada
places.story: In 1924 Alfonsina Strada rode the Giro d'Italia, the only woman ever to ride it with the men. She later ran a bicycle shop in Milan. The city named this street after her.

places.name: Rue Elsy Jacobs, Garnich
places.story: Elsy Jacobs of Luxembourg won the first women's road world championship, in 1958, and the same year set the first women's hour record. Garnich named this street after her.

places.name: The Mall, London
places.story: On 29 July 2012 Marianne Vos won the Olympic road race at the finish on The Mall, in pouring rain. She has won world titles on the road, on the track and in cyclocross.

places.name: Eileen Sheridan sculpture
places.story: Eileen Sheridan of Coventry rode from Land's End to John o' Groats in 1954 in less than two and a half days, a record. This artwork on the old railway path shows her beside the runner Dave Moorcroft.

places.name: Anna Meares Velodrome
places.story: Anna Meares won Olympic gold on the track in 2004 and 2012. The velodrome built for the 2018 Commonwealth Games carries her name.
